package.name: Uuid
package.description: UUID representation, parsing, formatting and generation

modules.name: Random
modules.header:
Random UUIDs, and the byte-order conversion that catches everyone.
A version 4 UUID is 122 bits of entropy with six bits spent on saying so: four for the version and two for
the variant. Those six are not wasted — they are what lets a reader tell a random UUID from a time-based one
without being told, and what keeps the two spaces from overlapping — but they do mean a version 4 UUID has
slightly less entropy than its size suggests, which matters only if someone is counting.
The GUID conversion is here because it is the single most common way UUIDs go wrong across a platform
boundary. Microsoft's GUID is the same sixteen bytes with the first three fields stored little-endian, so a
UUID written by a Windows API and read as a UUID — or the reverse — produces a value that is well-formed,
looks plausible, has the wrong version nibble in a place nobody checks, and refers to nothing. The conversion
is therefore a named function that must be called deliberately, never something applied automatically.

modules.name: Text
modules.header:
The text form, parsed strictly and written canonically.
RFC 9562 defines exactly one textual representation: thirty-two hexadecimal digits in five hyphen-separated
groups of 8-4-4-4-12, optionally prefixed by `urn:uuid:`. Everything else in circulation — the brace-wrapped
form Windows tools print, the hyphen-free form some databases store, upper case mixed with lower — is
something a program chose to accept, not something the standard blesses.
This parses strictly on purpose. A lenient parser is pleasant right up to the moment two systems disagree
about which strings are UUIDs, and then the disagreement is a security boundary: one accepts a string the
other rejects, or worse, two different strings map to one identifier. Accepting exactly one form means two
implementations of this cannot drift apart.
Case is the one exception, and it is asymmetric by design: both cases are *read*, because the standard says
they mean the same thing and rejecting upper case would break interoperation, but only lower case is
*written*, because RFC 9562 says output should be lower case and a canonical form that varies is not
canonical.
A refusal says where. The reason alone tells a caller what kind of mistake was made; the offset tells them which
character to point their own user at, which is the difference between "that is not a UUID" and an underline
under the character that is wrong. The offsets are into the text as given, so the URN form's digits are numbered
from the start of the whole string rather than from the start of the value inside it.
Writing refuses a destination too small rather than filling what fits. A truncated UUID is not a shorter UUID; it
is a different string, and one a strict parser refuses and a lenient one might not. The old writers stopped at
the end of the buffer and said nothing, so a caller who had miscounted got thirty of the thirty-six characters
and no way to learn it. Every writer here checks the room it needs before it writes a byte, so a refusal leaves
the destination exactly as it was and a success is always the complete form.

modules.name: TimeOrdered
modules.header:
Version 7: a UUID whose leading bits are a timestamp, so sorting the identifiers sorts the events.
The reason this version exists is databases. A version 4 UUID as a primary key scatters inserts across the
whole of a B-tree, so every insert dirties a different page and the index never stays in cache; a version 7
key appends, because its first six bytes are milliseconds since the Unix epoch, big-endian. The remaining
bits are random, which is what keeps it unguessable between milliseconds.
Within one millisecond the ordering is not guaranteed by the format — two UUIDs made in the same millisecond
have random tails and could sort either way. `MonotonicUuid` fixes that for a caller who needs it, by
remembering the last value it produced and stepping the random part forward when the clock has not moved. It
is a value the caller owns rather than a global, for the reason the random package gives at length: shared
mutable state makes results depend on who else is running.

modules.name: Uuid
modules.header:
A UUID: sixteen bytes, and the small amount of structure RFC 9562 gives them.
The bytes are held in the order the standard defines, which is the order they are written in and the order
they travel in on the wire. That is worth saying because Microsoft's GUID is the same sixteen bytes with the
first three fields byte-swapped, and a program reading one as the other gets a value that looks entirely
plausible and is wrong — so the conversion between them is explicit and lives in its own function rather
than happening implicitly anywhere.
Ordering is by the byte sequence, which for a version 7 UUID means ordering by time, since its timestamp sits
at the front in big-endian order. That is the whole reason version 7 exists, and it only works if comparison
never reorders the bytes.

doc.summary: A version 4 UUID drawn from the operating system's entropy.
doc.markdown:
A version 4 UUID drawn from the operating system's entropy.
Fails with why entropy was unavailable rather than producing a zero-filled UUID with the version bits set, which
would be a valid-looking identifier that is entirely predictable.
doc.returns: a version 4 value drawn from the system's generator, or why entropy was unavailable

doc.summary: A version 4 UUID built from sixteen bytes the caller supplies.
doc.markdown:
A version 4 UUID built from sixteen bytes the caller supplies.
For reproducing a UUID from a recorded seed, or for drawing from a generator other than the system's. The
version and variant bits are set regardless of what the bytes say, so the result is always a well-formed
version 4 UUID.

params.name: bytes
params.markdown: sixteen bytes to take as the value, in big-endian order

doc.returns: those bytes with the version and variant fields set for version 4

doc.summary: The same identifier with its first three fields byte-swapped, which is how Windows stores a GUID.
doc.markdown:
The same identifier with its first three fields byte-swapped, which is how Windows stores a GUID.
The conversion is its own inverse, so one function serves both directions: a UUID becomes the GUID bytes a
Windows API expects, and GUID bytes read from one become the UUID they represent. It must be called
deliberately — applying it by accident, or failing to apply it when crossing the boundary, both produce a
well-formed identifier that refers to something else entirely.
doc.returns: the same sixteen bytes with the first three fields byte-swapped

doc.summary: How long the canonical text form is: thirty-two digits and four hyphens.
doc.markdown: How long the canonical text form is: thirty-two digits and four hyphens.

doc.summary: How long the URN form is: the canonical form after `urn:uuid:`.
doc.markdown: How long the URN form is: the canonical form after `urn:uuid:`.

doc.summary: Why text could not be read as a UUID.
doc.markdown:
Why text could not be read as a UUID.
Failure-only: every case is a failure, and each carries the zero-based UTF-8 byte offset into the text where it
was found. Success is the other channel of `Uuid ! UuidParseError`, so there is no case here meaning nothing went
wrong.
Copy, carrying one offset and owning nothing.

cases.name: WrongLength
cases.doc:
The text is neither thirty-six characters nor forty-five with the URN prefix. The offset is the text's
length when it is too short, which is where the missing character would have gone, and the first character
the canonical form has no room for when it is too long.

cases.name: Misplaced
cases.doc:
A hyphen is missing where the form puts one, or one appears where a digit belongs. The offset is that
character.

cases.name: NotHexadecimal
cases.doc: A character that is not a hexadecimal digit. The offset is that character.

cases.name: BadPrefix
cases.doc:
The text has the length of the URN form but its `urn:uuid:` prefix is misspelled. The offset is the first
character that does not match.

doc.summary: Where in the input the failure was found.
doc.markdown:
Where in the input the failure was found.
Borrows the error and leaves it untouched. Cannot fail; runs in constant time and allocates nothing.
doc.returns: the zero-based UTF-8 byte offset, which is the text's length at end of input

items.name: Parse
items.signature: pub func Parse(text: char8[..]) -> Uuid ! UuidParseError

doc.summary: Reads a UUID from its canonical or URN text form.
doc.markdown:
Reads a UUID from its canonical or URN text form.
Both cases of the digits are accepted, because the standard says the two mean the same thing; nothing else is.
The URN prefix is compared case-insensitively, which is RFC 8141's rule for a scheme name and a different rule
from the digits — both are the standard's.
Reports `WrongLength` for text that is neither form's length, `BadPrefix` for a misspelled `urn:uuid:`,
`Misplaced` for a hyphen that is missing or one that stands where a digit belongs, and `NotHexadecimal` for any
other character that is not a digit. Each carries the byte offset into `text` where it was found. A refused
parse produces no value at all rather than a half-filled one.
doc.returns: the identifier, or why the text is not one

items.name: Parse
items.signature: pub func Parse(text: StringView) -> Uuid ! UuidParseError

doc.summary: Reads a UUID from the text a `StringView` borrows.
doc.markdown:
Reads a UUID from the text a `StringView` borrows.
The same parser, reached without the caller unwrapping the view first: a `StringView` is already validated
UTF-8, and a UUID's text is ASCII, so the bytes it borrows are exactly what the canonical form is made of.
The failures the slice form reports, with offsets into the borrowed text.
doc.returns: the identifier, or why the text is not one

items.name: Format
items.signature: pub func Format(value: &Uuid, into: var char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the canonical text form into `into`, in lower case.
doc.markdown:
Writes the canonical text form into `into`, in lower case.
Lower case because RFC 9562 says so, and because a canonical form that varies by case is not canonical — two
systems comparing text would disagree about equal UUIDs.
Reports `InsufficientCapacity` when `into` is shorter than `UuidTextLength`, leaving it exactly as it was. A
short destination is refused rather than filled with what fits, because a truncated UUID is a different string
rather than a shorter one. Room past the thirty-six characters is not touched.
doc.returns: success when the whole form was written

items.name: FormatUpper
items.signature: pub func FormatUpper(value: &Uuid, into: var char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the canonical text form into `into`, in upper case.
doc.markdown:
Writes the canonical text form into `into`, in upper case.
Offered because some formats demand it; `Format` is what a program should write when it has the choice.
The failure `Format` reports, for the same reason and with the same guarantee.
doc.returns: success when the whole form was written

items.name: FormatUrn
items.signature: pub func FormatUrn(value: &Uuid, into: var char8[..]) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the URN form into `into`: the canonical form after `urn:uuid:`.
doc.markdown:
Writes the URN form into `into`: the canonical form after `urn:uuid:`.
Reports `InsufficientCapacity` when `into` is shorter than `UuidUrnLength`, leaving it exactly as it was. The
form is refused whole, so a destination never receives a prefix with nothing after it.
doc.returns: success when the whole form was written

doc.summary: A version 7 UUID: the current time in its leading bits, entropy in the rest.
doc.markdown:
A version 7 UUID: the current time in its leading bits, entropy in the rest.
Fails with why entropy was unavailable rather than producing a timestamp-shaped value with no randomness — which
would be guessable and would look fine.
doc.returns: a version 7 value carrying the current time, or why entropy was unavailable

items.name: TimeOrderedAt
items.signature: pub func TimeOrderedAt(milliseconds: uint64) -> Uuid ! EntropyError

doc.summary: A version 7 UUID for a given millisecond, with entropy in the rest.
doc.markdown:
A version 7 UUID for a given millisecond, with entropy in the rest.
For reproducing an identifier from a recorded time, and for testing.

params.name: milliseconds
params.markdown: the timestamp to embed, in milliseconds since the Unix epoch

doc.returns: a version 7 value carrying `milliseconds`, or why entropy was unavailable

doc.summary: The millisecond a version 7 UUID carries.
doc.markdown:
The millisecond a version 7 UUID carries.
Meaningless for any other version, which is why the version should be checked first.
doc.returns: the timestamp a version 7 value carries; meaningless for any other version

doc.summary: A generator of version 7 UUIDs that are strictly increasing, even within one millisecond.
doc.markdown:
A generator of version 7 UUIDs that are strictly increasing, even within one millisecond.
The format guarantees ordering only between milliseconds; two UUIDs made in the same one have random tails
and may sort either way. This closes that by remembering the last value it produced: when the clock has not
advanced, it increments the previous UUID instead of drawing a fresh one, so every value it returns is
strictly greater than the last.
A caller owns one of these rather than sharing a global, so two components generating identifiers do not
serialize against each other or interleave into one sequence.

fields.name: previous
fields.doc: The last value returned, or nil before the first.

fields.name: started
fields.doc: Whether anything has been returned yet.

doc.summary: A generator that has produced nothing yet.
doc.markdown: A generator that has produced nothing yet.
doc.returns: the generator, which has produced nothing yet

members.name: WriteDisplay
members.signature: pub func WriteDisplay(self: &Uuid, writer: &var TextWriter, spec: FormatSpec) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: Writes the canonical lower-case form, or the URN form under the `urn` style.
doc.markdown:
Writes the canonical lower-case form, or the URN form under the `urn` style.
The default is the hyphenated form RFC 9562 defines, in lower case, because that is the one representation
the standard has and the one every other implementation writes. `hyphenated` names it explicitly and `urn`
selects the `urn:uuid:` form. Upper case is not a style, since a canonical form that varies by case is not
canonical; `FormatUpper` remains for a format that demands it.
Reports whatever the writer reported, and `UnsupportedRequest` for any other style or for a precision, which
a value of exactly one length has nothing to apply.
doc.returns: success when the whole form was accepted

members.signature: pub func WriteDebug(self: &Uuid, writer: &var TextWriter, spec: FormatSpec) -> ! FormatError

doc.summary: The same text as `Display`: an identifier has one reading, and quoting it would say nothing extra.
doc.markdown:
The same text as `Display`: an identifier has one reading, and quoting it would say nothing extra.
The failures `WriteDisplay` reports.
doc.returns: success when the whole form was accepted

doc.summary: The nil UUID: sixteen zero bytes.
doc.markdown:
The nil UUID: sixteen zero bytes.
A defined value rather than an absence, and worth having as one — the alternative is every caller
inventing a sentinel of their own.
doc.returns: the all-zero value

doc.summary: The max UUID: sixteen bytes of ones, which RFC 9562 defines as nil's counterpart.
doc.markdown: The max UUID: sixteen bytes of ones, which RFC 9562 defines as nil's counterpart.
doc.returns: the all-ones value

doc.summary: A UUID from sixteen bytes in the standard's order.
doc.markdown:
A UUID from sixteen bytes in the standard's order.
Fewer than sixteen leaves the rest zero; more are ignored. No structure is imposed — the version and
variant fields are whatever the bytes say, which is what lets this read a UUID from somewhere else.

params.name: bytes
params.markdown: sixteen bytes to take as the value, in big-endian order

doc.returns: those sixteen bytes as a value, with no field interpreted or corrected

doc.summary: The sixteen bytes, in the standard's order.
doc.markdown: The sixteen bytes, in the standard's order.
doc.returns: the sixteen bytes, in big-endian order

doc.summary: Whether this is the nil UUID.
doc.markdown: Whether this is the nil UUID.
doc.returns: whether every byte is zero

doc.summary: Whether this is the max UUID.
doc.markdown: Whether this is the max UUID.
doc.returns: whether every byte is one

doc.summary: The version, from the high nibble of the seventh byte.
doc.markdown:
The version, from the high nibble of the seventh byte.
Meaningful only for the standard variant; a nil or max UUID reports a number that means nothing, which
is why `Variant` should be consulted first.
doc.returns: the version nibble, 0 through 15; a value this package did not make may hold anything

doc.summary: The variant, from the high bits of the ninth byte.
doc.markdown:
The variant, from the high bits of the ninth byte.
The encoding is variable-length rather than two fixed bits: a leading zero means the oldest layout, `10`
the standard one, `110` Microsoft's, and `111` the reserved future.
doc.returns: the variant the layout declares

doc.summary: Whether two UUIDs are the same.
doc.markdown: Whether two UUIDs are the same.
doc.returns: whether all sixteen bytes match

doc.summary: Orders two UUIDs by their bytes, most significant first.
doc.markdown:
Orders two UUIDs by their bytes, most significant first.
For a version 7 UUID this is chronological order, because its timestamp occupies the leading bytes in
big-endian form. Reordering here — to match a platform's GUID layout, say — would destroy that, which
is why the byte order is fixed rather than negotiable.
doc.returns: how the two order as sixteen big-endian bytes, which is lexicographic order for the text

doc.summary: A hash of the sixteen bytes, for use as a table key.
doc.markdown:
A hash of the sixteen bytes, for use as a table key.
FNV-1a, which is not a cryptographic hash and does not need to be: a UUID is already the output of one,
or of an entropy source, so what a table wants here is speed and an even spread over buckets.
doc.returns: the value's hash

doc.summary: What layout a UUID's bytes follow.
doc.markdown: What layout a UUID's bytes follow.

cases.doc: Apollo NCS, from before the standard — the layout the nil UUID also happens to match.

cases.name: Standard
cases.doc: The layout RFC 9562 defines, which is what essentially every UUID in use is.

cases.name: Microsoft
cases.doc: Microsoft's early variant: reserved, and rare.

cases.name: Future
